questions.stem: What are the three main types of rock?
questions.explanation: The three types are defined by how they formed, not by how they look or feel.

questions.stem: How does igneous rock form?
options: From layers of sediment pressed together
From heat and pressure changing existing rock
From cooling and solidifying molten rock
questions.explanation: Igneous comes from the Latin for fire. Granite and basalt are examples.

questions.stem: How does sedimentary rock form?
options: From layers of sediment compacted and cemented over time
questions.explanation: Sandstone and limestone form this way, which is why fossils are usually found in sedimentary rock.

questions.stem: How does metamorphic rock form?
options: Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting
Sediment settles on a sea floor
questions.explanation: If it melted completely it would become igneous instead. Marble and slate are metamorphic.

questions.stem: What is the theory of plate tectonics?
options: Earth's surface is a single unbroken shell
Earth's outer layer is broken into plates that move slowly
questions.explanation: Plate movement explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building together, which is why it is such a powerful theory.

questions.stem: What usually happens at a convergent plate boundary?
options: Plates move towards each other and may form mountains or trenches
Plates move apart and new crust forms
The plates lock together and stop moving permanently
questions.explanation: Converging plates collide. Divergent boundaries pull apart and transform boundaries slide.

questions.stem: What happens at a divergent plate boundary?
options: Plates move apart and new crust forms between them
Plates slide sideways past each other
questions.explanation: Mid-ocean ridges form where plates separate and magma rises to fill the gap.

questions.stem: What is a transform plate boundary?
options: Where plates slide past one another horizontally
questions.explanation: Transform boundaries produce earthquakes but usually no volcanoes. The San Andreas Fault is the best-known example.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Coal takes millions of years to form, so on human timescales it is not replaced.
questions.teaching:
Non-renewable resources are those that cannot be replaced on any timescale that matters to people.

Fossil fuels are the clearest case: coal, oil and natural gas formed from organisms buried and compressed over hundreds of millions of years, so burning them removes them permanently. Mineral ores and metals are also finite, although these can often be recycled, which is a real difference from fuels — once a fuel is burnt, the energy is dispersed and cannot be recovered.

questions.stem: What is magma?
options: Molten rock that has erupted onto the surface
questions.explanation: Once it reaches the surface it is called lava. Same material, different name by location.

questions.stem: What is weathering?
options: The breaking down of rock where it sits
The movement of broken rock to a new place
The formation of new rock from magma
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock down in place; erosion transports the pieces away.

questions.stem: What is erosion?
options: The transport of weathered material by wind, water or ice
The breaking down of rock in place
questions.explanation: Erosion moves material. Weathering breaks it up first.

questions.stem: Where are fossils most commonly found?
questions.explanation: Sediment can bury remains gently. The heat of igneous and metamorphic formation destroys fossils.
questions.teaching:
Rocks form in three ways, and only one of them can preserve the remains of living things.

Igneous rock forms from cooling molten material, which destroys anything organic. Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is altered by heat and pressure, which usually destroys any fossils present. The third type forms as particles settle in layers and are compressed over time — gently enough that remains buried in those layers can survive. That is why fossil hunting means looking for layered rock such as sandstone, shale and limestone.

questions.stem: What is the rock cycle?
options: The movement of rocks down a hill
The set of processes that change rock from one type into another over time
The daily heating and cooling of rocks
The way rocks are mined and used
questions.explanation: Rock is continually recycled between the three types over geological time.

questions.stem: Which layer of Earth do tectonic plates form part of?
questions.explanation: Plates are sections of the rigid lithosphere, which sits on the slowly flowing mantle beneath.
questions.teaching:
Earth is layered, and the layers can be described either by what they are made of or by how they behave.

By composition the divisions are crust, mantle and core. By behaviour the outer part is split differently: a rigid outer shell made of the crust plus the uppermost mantle, sitting on a weaker, partly mobile layer beneath called the asthenosphere. Tectonic plates are pieces of that rigid outer shell, which is why a plate contains both crust and mantle material — a point the compositional layers alone do not explain.

questions.stem: What causes most earthquakes?
options: Sudden movement along faults where plates meet
The Moon's gravity pulling on rocks
questions.explanation: Stress builds along plate boundaries and releases suddenly as an earthquake.

questions.stem: Which of these is a renewable energy resource?
questions.explanation: Wind is continually replenished. The other three are fossil fuels.
questions.teaching:
The dividing line is whether a resource replenishes fast enough to keep using it indefinitely.

Energy from the Sun, from moving air, from flowing or falling water, from tides and from the Earth's internal heat all pass, because they keep arriving regardless of how much is used. Fossil fuels fail, because they took hundreds of millions of years to form. Biomass sits in between: renewable if regrown as fast as it is burnt, and not if it is not. Being clean and being renewable are separate questions, though they often go together.

questions.stem: What are fossil fuels formed from?
options: The remains of organisms buried over millions of years
questions.explanation: Coal, oil and gas all formed from ancient organic material under heat and pressure over vast timescales.

questions.stem: What is a mineral?
options: A naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical composition
Any solid found in the ground
questions.explanation: Rocks are made of minerals. Quartz and feldspar are minerals; granite is a rock containing them.

questions.stem: Why does the rock cycle operate over very different timescales?
options: All rock processes take exactly the same time
Only igneous rock takes time to form
The cycle takes exactly one million years
Some processes such as weathering act quickly while burial and metamorphism take millions of years
questions.explanation: Timescale variation is explicitly part of the curriculum here: a lava flow solidifies in days, while deep burial and uplift take millions of years.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the theory of plate tectonics?
options: Matching rock types and fossils on coastlines now separated by ocean
questions.explanation: Matching geology and fossils across oceans is strong evidence of former connection — the core of Wegener's original case.

questions.stem: Why do volcanoes and earthquakes cluster in the same regions?
options: Both occur mainly along plate boundaries
questions.explanation: The shared cause is plate interaction. This clustering is what first suggested the plates exist.

questions.stem: A rock has visible layers and contains shell fragments. What type is it and why?
options: Sedimentary, because layers and fossils indicate deposition
questions.explanation: Layering plus fossils is characteristic of sediment settling over time. Metamorphic banding is a different pattern and rarely preserves shells.

questions.stem: Why is the sustainable use of a resource about the rate of use, not just the amount available?
options: Supply depends only on the total amount in the ground
A renewable resource can still be exhausted if used faster than it is replaced
Amount available is impossible to measure
Renewable resources can never run out
questions.explanation: Overfishing and groundwater depletion are both cases of renewable resources being used unsustainably.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine risk of extracting a mineral resource?
options: Habitat disturbance and contamination of water from mine waste
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks for both benefits and risks. Land disturbance and water contamination are the main environmental risks.

questions.stem: Why does the sea floor get older with distance from a mid-ocean ridge?
options: Rock cools more slowly further from the ridge, ageing it faster
Sediment ages faster near the coast
New crust forms at the ridge and moves outwards over time
Older rock sinks towards the ridge
questions.explanation: Sea-floor spreading produces a symmetrical age pattern either side of the ridge — one of the strongest pieces of evidence for plate tectonics.

questions.stem: A metamorphic rock shows banding. What does this suggest about its formation?
options: Minerals were rearranged under directed pressure
questions.explanation: Bands form as minerals align under pressure. Sedimentary layers form differently, by deposition.

questions.stem: Why is the depth of a sedimentary layer sometimes used to estimate time?
options: Sediment accumulates at a roughly steady rate in stable conditions
All layers form in exactly one year
A thicker layer always represents a shorter period
questions.explanation: Rate of deposition allows estimation, but conditions change, so it is an estimate, not a clock. Deeper layers are older, not younger.

questions.stem: Which statement about coal formation is correct?
options: It forms in a few decades from any buried material
It forms from evaporating sea water
It formed from plant material buried and compressed over millions of years
questions.explanation: The timescale is exactly why coal is non-renewable in human terms.

questions.stem: Why was Wegener's idea of continental drift initially rejected?
options: The continents clearly do not fit together
He could not explain a mechanism that could move continents
questions.explanation: The evidence was suggestive but the missing mechanism was a legitimate scientific objection. Sea-floor spreading later supplied it — a good example of how theories become accepted.

questions.stem: Which discovery most strengthened the case for plate tectonics in the 1960s?
options: The discovery of new fossil species
Magnetic striping in sea-floor rocks recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field
questions.explanation: Symmetrical magnetic stripes either side of ridges demonstrated the sea floor was spreading — the mechanism Wegener lacked.

questions.stem: Why can the same atoms of rock appear in all three rock types over geological time?
options: New atoms are created in each rock type
The rock cycle recycles material through melting, deposition and metamorphism
Atoms change type as rocks change
questions.explanation: The material is conserved and reused; only its arrangement and history change.

questions.stem: Which argument best supports moving from a non-renewable to a renewable energy source?
options: Non-renewable supplies are finite and their extraction and use carry environmental costs
Renewable generation needs no land, materials or maintenance
questions.explanation: The honest case rests on finite supply plus environmental cost. Overstating it — 'no drawbacks', 'already exhausted' — is not supportable.

questions.stem: Two mountain ranges have similar rock and fossils but sit on different continents. What is the best explanation?
options: The rocks formed independently by coincidence
The fossils were carried by birds
The mountains are the same age by chance
The continents were once joined and have since separated
questions.explanation: Shared geology across an ocean is the classic evidence for former connection, seen in the Appalachians and Scottish Highlands.

questions.stem: Why does deep burial change a rock without melting it?
options: Increased pressure and moderate heat rearrange minerals in the solid state
Pressure lowers the melting point until the rock liquefies
questions.explanation: Metamorphism happens below the melting point. Complete melting would produce igneous rock on cooling instead.

questions.stem: Which observation would most challenge the claim that a valley was carved by a glacier?
options: The valley is in a cold region
The valley has a narrow V-shaped cross-section rather than a U-shape
questions.explanation: Glaciers carve broad U-shaped valleys; rivers cut V-shaped ones. Cross-section is the diagnostic feature.

questions.stem: Why is recycling metal usually less damaging than mining new ore?
options: Recycled metal needs no transport before reuse
It avoids the land disturbance and waste of extraction and uses less energy
Recycled metal is chemically purer than mined metal
questions.explanation: The metal atoms are the same either way; recycling simply skips the extraction stage and its costs.

questions.stem: What is lava?
options: Molten rock that has reached the Earth's surface
questions.explanation: Underground it is magma; once it erupts it is lava.

questions.stem: What is a fossil?
options: Preserved remains or traces of a once-living organism
questions.explanation: Fossils include bones, shells, footprints and burrows.
questions.teaching:
Fossilisation is rare. Most organisms decay completely, so the fossil record is a thin and patchy sample rather than a full catalogue — usually only hard parts, and usually only where the remains were buried quickly in sediment.

Two kinds turn up. Some are the organism itself, or the minerals that gradually replaced it: bones, shells, teeth, wood. Others are marks the organism left behind while alive — footprints, burrows, droppings — which record behaviour rather than anatomy. Both count. What does not count is any old buried rock: age and depth alone do not make something one of these, and the link to a living thing is the whole point.

questions.stem: What is sediment?
options: Small particles of rock and organic material that settle out
questions.explanation: Sediment is deposited by water, wind or ice and can later become sedimentary rock.

questions.stem: What is the crust of the Earth?
options: The layer of air above the surface
questions.explanation: The crust is thin compared with the mantle beneath it.

questions.stem: What is the mantle?
options: The Earth's outer shell of plates
The thick layer beneath the crust that flows very slowly
questions.explanation: Slow convection in the mantle is thought to drive plate movement.

questions.stem: What is a volcano?
options: An opening where magma, gas and ash reach the surface
questions.explanation: Not all mountains are volcanoes — many form by collision and uplift.

questions.stem: What is a tsunami usually caused by?
options: A sudden displacement of the sea floor, often by an earthquake
questions.explanation: Tsunamis are generated by sudden vertical movement of water, not by weather.

questions.stem: Which resource is renewable?
questions.explanation: Flowing water is continually replenished by the water cycle.
questions.teaching:
Resources are classified by whether using them today reduces what is available tomorrow.

Renewable ones are replaced naturally on a human timescale — sunlight, wind, flowing water, and heat from underground. Non-renewable ones formed over hundreds of millions of years and are effectively gone once used, which covers coal, oil, natural gas and mineral ores. The test is the rate of replacement, not how much remains: coal is abundant and still non-renewable, because nothing is making more of it at any useful pace.

questions.stem: What is an ore?
options: A rock containing enough of a metal to be worth extracting
questions.explanation: The word implies economic viability, not just presence.

questions.stem: What does uplift mean in geology?
options: The raising of land by tectonic forces
questions.explanation: Uplift can expose deeply buried rock at the surface over long periods.

questions.stem: Why are fossils rarely found in igneous rock?
options: The heat of molten rock destroys organic remains
Igneous rock forms too deep for remains to reach
Igneous rock cools too quickly for remains to be buried
questions.explanation: Fossilisation needs gentle burial, which sediment provides and magma does not.

questions.stem: Two rock layers are undisturbed. Which is older?
questions.explanation: The principle of superposition: in undisturbed layers, older material lies beneath younger.

questions.stem: Why does mountain building often occur at convergent boundaries?
options: Colliding plates crumple and thicken the crust
Plates slide past each other, lifting rock
questions.explanation: The Himalayas continue to rise from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates.

questions.stem: Why does a deep ocean trench form where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate?
options: Sediment builds up into a trench
The denser oceanic plate is forced down beneath the continental plate
questions.explanation: Subduction of the denser plate creates the trench and often a volcanic arc behind it.

questions.stem: Why is coal described as stored solar energy?
options: It is heated by the Sun
It formed from plants that captured sunlight by photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Burning coal releases energy that plants captured hundreds of millions of years ago.

questions.stem: Which best explains why some rocks contain rounded pebbles?
options: They were transported by water, which wore the edges away
They cooled from magma in that shape
They were shaped by heat and pressure
questions.explanation: Roundness records transport distance, which is why conglomerates indicate a river or beach environment.

questions.stem: Why does recycling aluminium save a large amount of energy?
options: Recycled aluminium needs no heating at all
Aluminium ore lies close to the surface and is cheap to reach
Recycling removes the need to transport the metal
Extracting aluminium from ore requires far more energy than remelting it
questions.explanation: Primary extraction is extremely energy-intensive, so recycling saves the bulk of that cost.

questions.stem: What does the presence of marine fossils on a mountain top suggest?
options: The mountain was once flooded briefly
The fossils were carried by wind
Rock formed under the sea has since been uplifted
questions.explanation: It records both deposition in a marine environment and later tectonic uplift.

questions.stem: Why do earthquakes occur along the San Andreas Fault?
options: Two plates slide past each other and stress releases suddenly
questions.explanation: It is a transform boundary, which produces earthquakes without the volcanism of convergent zones.

questions.stem: Why can the age of a rock layer be estimated from the fossils it contains?
options: Fossils decay at a fixed rate
All fossils are the same age
Certain species existed only during known intervals, so they date the layer
questions.explanation: Index fossils are widespread, abundant and short-lived, making them useful time markers.

questions.stem: Why is the rock cycle described as a cycle rather than a sequence?
options: It always follows the same fixed order
Rock can move between the three types repeatedly and in different orders
questions.explanation: There is no fixed starting point — igneous rock can metamorphose directly, sediment can be melted, and so on.

questions.stem: A mineral resource is described as economically viable. What does this depend on?
options: Concentration, extraction cost and the market price of the material
How deep the deposit is only
questions.explanation: A deposit can become viable when prices rise or extraction technology improves, without the rock changing at all.

questions.stem: Which argument best supports leaving some fossil fuel reserves unextracted?
options: Extraction and use carry climate and environmental costs that may exceed the benefits
Burning them releases no carbon if done efficiently
questions.explanation: The case rests on weighing costs against benefits, which is exactly what the curriculum asks students to do.

questions.stem: What would most challenge the claim that a rock is sedimentary?
options: Finding interlocking crystals with no layering or grains
questions.explanation: Interlocking crystals indicate cooling from a melt, which points to igneous origin.

questions.stem: What is the outer core of the Earth made of?
options: Liquid metal, mainly iron and nickel
questions.explanation: Movement in the liquid outer core generates Earth's magnetic field.

questions.stem: What is the inner core of the Earth?
options: A solid metal sphere under enormous pressure
questions.explanation: Despite extreme heat, pressure keeps the inner core solid.

questions.stem: What is a mineral's hardness?
questions.explanation: The Mohs scale ranks minerals by scratch resistance.
questions.teaching:
Minerals are identified by testing their physical properties, and each test targets a different property.

Streak is the colour of the powder left when rubbed on a tile. Lustre describes how the surface reflects light. Density compares mass to volume. Cleavage describes how it breaks. And one test measures how well it resists being marked by something else, ranked on Mohs' scale from talc at one to diamond at ten — where each mineral can scratch those below it and not those above. Geologists use a fingernail, a coin and a steel blade as rough reference points.

questions.stem: What is a sedimentary rock made of limestone mainly formed from?
questions.explanation: Shells and coral fragments accumulate and compact over time.

questions.stem: What is a seismograph used to measure?
questions.explanation: Seismographs record vibrations, allowing magnitude and location to be determined.
questions.teaching:
Earthquakes release energy as waves through the ground, and instruments are designed to detect and record them.

The instrument works on inertia: a suspended mass tends to stay still while the frame around it moves with the ground, and recording the relative movement produces a trace. Comparing traces from several stations lets geologists locate an earthquake's origin, since different wave types travel at different speeds. The magnitude scale is derived from these recordings, and being logarithmic, each step up represents about thirty times more energy released.

questions.stem: What is subduction?
options: One tectonic plate sinking beneath another
questions.explanation: Subduction produces deep trenches and volcanic activity.

questions.stem: What is a mid-ocean ridge?
options: An underwater mountain range where plates move apart
questions.explanation: New oceanic crust forms along the ridge as magma rises.

questions.stem: What is coal mainly formed from?
questions.explanation: Ancient swamp vegetation buried under sediment became coal over millions of years.
questions.teaching:
Fossil fuels are named for their origin: they formed from the remains of living things buried long ago.

One of them formed in ancient swamps and forests, where plant material accumulated faster than it could rot. Buried under sediment and subjected to heat and pressure over hundreds of millions of years, it lost water and gases and became progressively richer in carbon. Oil and natural gas formed the same way but mainly from marine organisms in ancient seas. Knowing which organisms each came from explains why they are found in different rock formations.

questions.stem: What is a non-renewable energy resource?
options: One that cannot be replaced within a human timescale
questions.explanation: Timescale of replacement is the defining feature.

questions.stem: Why do volcanic islands often form in chains?
options: Volcanoes migrate across the sea floor
Sediment builds up along a fault line
Each eruption pushes the next volcano further along
A plate moves over a stationary hot spot, producing volcanoes in sequence
questions.explanation: The Hawaiian chain is the classic example, with age increasing away from the active volcano.

questions.stem: Why are the oldest sea-floor rocks much younger than the oldest continental rocks?
options: Oceanic crust is continually recycled by subduction
questions.explanation: Continental crust is buoyant and persists; oceanic crust is destroyed and renewed.

questions.stem: How does the rock cycle connect igneous and sedimentary rock?
options: Igneous rock weathers into sediment that can form sedimentary rock, which can melt again
Igneous rock forms first and sedimentary rock forms afterwards, in a sequence that runs one way only
Both types form from magma, but sedimentary rock cools more slowly and so ends up in layers
Sedimentary rock is compressed into igneous rock by the weight of the layers above it over time
questions.explanation: Material moves in both directions over geological time.

questions.stem: Why is groundwater extraction sometimes unsustainable?
options: Extraction pulls water in from neighbouring aquifers
Some aquifers recharge far more slowly than water is removed
questions.explanation: The rate of recharge, not the total volume, determines sustainability.

questions.stem: Why does metamorphic rock often form near plate boundaries?
options: Metamorphic rock only forms at the surface
Collision generates the heat and pressure required
questions.explanation: The conditions needed for metamorphism concentrate where plates interact.

questions.stem: Why is rehabilitating a mine site important?
options: It returns the site to exactly its original ecosystem
It restores land and reduces long-term environmental harm
questions.explanation: Rehabilitation addresses the lasting impact of extraction after production ends.

questions.stem: Why does the age pattern of sea-floor rocks support plate tectonics so strongly?
options: It shows the Earth is old
It shows the ocean basins have been shrinking over time
The symmetrical increase in age away from ridges is predicted by sea-floor spreading and by nothing else
questions.explanation: A theory gains support when it predicts a specific, otherwise unexpected pattern that is then observed.

questions.stem: Why can a rock's mineral composition indicate the conditions under which it formed?
options: All rocks contain the same minerals
Particular minerals are stable only within certain temperature and pressure ranges
questions.explanation: Index minerals let geologists infer the depth and temperature of formation.

questions.stem: Why is the geological timescale divided by major changes in fossil records?
options: The divisions cover equal spans of time
Sharp changes in life mark significant events that are recognisable worldwide
The divisions follow changes in rock type alone
The divisions were fixed by early geologists' surveys
questions.explanation: Mass extinctions and radiations provide globally correlatable boundaries.

questions.stem: A rock contains rounded grains cemented together with fossils between them. Which formation history fits?
options: Transported sediment deposited in water, buried and cemented
Direct crystallisation from a magma chamber
questions.explanation: Rounding indicates transport, and fossil preservation indicates gentle deposition.
